characters: Grace Sefa: a 14-year-old girl in a school uniform, holding a small glass bottle labelled “insulin”.
Papa Jacob: her grandfather, in his seventies, in a cardigan, with a kind smile and a small injection kit.
Mr Enchill: the science teacher, in a lab coat, with a diagram of a bacterium and a DNA loop.
The bacterium: a tiny rod-shaped microbe drawn very large on a board with a small circle of DNA inside.

narrationPlan.voice: Curious girl’s voice for Grace; a kind, patient voice for Papa Jacob; a clear voice for Mr Enchill
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and gentle, slowing for the science (about 118 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Quiet laboratory hum with a soft piano; a wondering, rising theme at the big idea (placeholder)
culturalNotes: Grace, Papa Jacob and Mr Enchill are invented. The science facts are from published sources: before genetic engineering, insulin came from the pancreas of pigs and cows (about ten thousand pounds of pancreas for one pound of crystals in 1923); in 1973 researchers showed that genes can be moved between bacteria; the first human insulin made in bacteria was approved in 1982; a heat-stable enzyme from Yellowstone bacteria made PCR practical; artemisinin came from sweet wormwood and the 2015 Nobel committee estimated it saves over 100,000 lives a year in Africa.

The nibima (Cryptolepis sanguinolenta) lines report laboratory findings only; no human clinical trial result is claimed. The story warns that no one should replace proper malaria treatment with a plant.

The idea that “everything should be kept because we cannot know what will be useful” is shown as the precaution argument, with an honest note that most species will not become medicines and that there are other strong reasons to protect them.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Have a biology teacher check the simplified description of how insulin is made with bacteria and how PCR works.
Check the separate penicillin example (Fleming, 1928; Penicillium mould killing nearby Staphylococcus bacteria) and the description of insulin as a key for cells with a reliable source.
Check that the diabetes details are accurate and respectful, that the story does not give medical advice, and that families affected by diabetes are not alarmed.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about insulin, bacteria and the precaution argument for protecting biodiversity. It models explanatory writing with sequence words.
learningGoals: Explain in order how human insulin is made using bacteria.
Give three examples of useful discoveries from wild living things.
Explain the precaution argument and why it is not the only reason to protect species.
beforeReading: Ask: which living things have you seen that might one day help people?
whileReading: At page 7, ask learners to rank the three reasons for protecting species.
afterReading: Write a process paragraph on how a seed grows, using sequence words.
Research one medicine that came from a plant, mould or microbe.
discussion: Is “we may need it one day” a good reason to protect a species? What other reasons are there?
What does it mean that extinction is permanent?
reflection: What is one living thing near you that you would like to protect and why?

support: Provide a process frame: First… Next… Then… After that… Finally…
stretch: Write a short article for the school magazine on why scientists study hot springs.

localiseThis: Use real local plants and the research of your regional university; never recommend a plant as medicine without professional advice.

factCheck.claim: Human insulin made in bacteria was first achieved in 1978 by a Genentech and City of Hope team, and the first such medicine (Humulin) was approved in 1982; before that insulin came from the pancreas of pigs and cows.
factCheck.explanation: From the US National Science Foundation’s account of recombinant insulin.

factCheck.claim: A heat-stable enzyme (Taq) from a Yellowstone hot-spring bacterium was isolated about a decade after the 1964 discovery of the bacterium, and became the basis of PCR.
factCheck.explanation: From the US National Science Foundation’s account of PCR.

factCheck.claim: Artemisinin, from sweet wormwood, was discovered by Tu Youyou’s team after a search of ancient texts; she shared the 2015 Nobel Prize; the Nobel committee estimated over 100,000 lives saved each year in Africa; resistance has emerged in Southeast Asia.
factCheck.explanation: From a PBS NewsHour report on the 2015 prize.
factCheck.reference: PBS NewsHour, “Chinese herbal therapy for malaria wins part of Nobel Prize in medicine” (pbs.org/newshour).
